_comment: Research OS for K-12, Phase 0 seed path: why is the sky blue. See _intake/research-os-k12/RESEARCH-OS-K12-SYSTEM-REVIEW.md section 8 (Phase 0 prototype slice: one canon branch, 02-physics; grades 3-5 up to Rayleigh scattering; 15-25 nodes). Loaded by scripts/seed-research-os.mjs. Every provenance entry is a verified real source: NASA Space Place and Wikipedia for the grade-level facts, the Tyndall 1869 and Rayleigh 1871 papers (DOIs confirmed by resolving doi.org to the publisher record) for the primary-source and law tiers. bkt-ros ros-14: a node may also carry an optional worked_example ({text, source}), an authored (not verbatim) grade-4-level model explanation of the node's own idea plus the source it rests on, shown to a low-prior-knowledge learner before their own explanation box (learning/research-os/GUIDANCE.md). Seeded on this path's first six nodes only.

nodes.title: Light travels in straight lines
nodes.summary: Light moves in a straight path until it hits something that reflects it, bends it, or scatters it.

worked_example.text: Light travels in a straight line, like a laser pointer beam. It keeps going straight until it hits something. When it hits something, it can bounce off (reflect), bend, or scatter in a new direction.
worked_example.source: NASA Space Place (2024). Why Is the Sky Blue?.

nodes.title: Sunlight looks white
nodes.summary: Sunlight looks white to our eyes, even though, as later nodes show, it is a mix of every visible color.

worked_example.text: Sunlight looks plain white to our eyes, like one simple color. That is only how it looks. White sunlight is a mix of every color of light put together.
worked_example.source: NASA Space Place (2024). Why Is the Sky Blue?.

nodes.title: Air is made of tiny particles
nodes.summary: Air is made of countless tiny particles, mostly nitrogen and oxygen molecules, far too small to see.

worked_example.text: The air around us looks empty, but it is not. Air is packed with tiny particles, mostly nitrogen and oxygen molecules. These particles are so small that no one can see just one with their own eyes.
worked_example.source: NASA Space Place (2024). Why Is the Sky Blue?.

nodes.title: White light splits into colors
nodes.summary: White light can split into the colors of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet, the way a prism or raindrop shows.

worked_example.text: White light looks like one color, but it is a mix. A prism or a raindrop can split white light apart. Once split, you see red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet, the colors of a rainbow.
worked_example.source: NASA Space Place (2024). Why Is the Sky Blue?.

nodes.title: Each color is a wavelength
nodes.summary: Each color of light has its own wavelength. Red light has a longer wavelength; blue and violet light have shorter wavelengths.

worked_example.text: Every color of light travels as a wave, and each wave has a length, called a wavelength. Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light. Blue and violet light have the shortest wavelengths of the colors we can see.

nodes.title: Light can scatter off small things
nodes.summary: When light meets something much smaller than itself, some of the light bounces off in new directions instead of continuing straight. This is called scattering.

worked_example.text: Light usually travels straight, without stopping. But when light hits something much smaller than itself, part of the light bounces off in a new direction instead of going straight. Scientists call this bouncing-off scattering.
worked_example.source: NASA Space Place (2024). Why Is the Sky Blue?.

nodes.title: Waves have wavelength and frequency
nodes.summary: A wave repeats itself in space. The distance between two repeats is its wavelength; a shorter wavelength means more repeats fit into the same distance.

nodes.title: Visible light is part of the electromagnetic spectrum
nodes.summary: Visible light is a narrow band, about 380 to 750 nanometers, inside the much larger electromagnetic spectrum that also includes radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet, and X-rays.

nodes.title: Blue and violet have the shortest visible wavelengths
nodes.summary: Among visible colors, violet and blue sit at the short-wavelength end (about 380-500 nm) and red sits at the long-wavelength end (about 625-750 nm).

nodes.title: Light travels as a wave
nodes.summary: Light travels as an electromagnetic wave, and how it interacts with matter depends on the relation between its wavelength and the size of what it meets.

nodes.title: Air molecules are much smaller than light's wavelength
nodes.summary: Nitrogen and oxygen molecules, roughly a few tenths of a nanometer across, are thousands of times smaller than visible-light wavelengths (about 400-700 nm).

nodes.title: Tyndall's experiments on scattering by small particles
nodes.summary: John Tyndall showed experimentally that light scattered by small particles suspended in a clear medium comes out bluish and polarized, tying a scattered blue color to scattering by particles far smaller than the light's wavelength.

provenance.author: John Tyndall
provenance.title: On the blue colour of the sky, the polarization of skylight, and on the polarization of light by cloudy matter generally
provenance.publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London

nodes.title: Scattering strength depends on particle size versus wavelength
nodes.summary: How strongly a particle scatters light, and how that scattering depends on wavelength, changes with the particle's size relative to the wavelength. Particles much smaller than the wavelength, like air molecules, scatter short wavelengths far more strongly than long ones.

nodes.title: Rayleigh's 1871 papers on the light from the sky
nodes.summary: Lord Rayleigh's 1871 papers derived the polarization and color of skylight from scattering by particles much smaller than the light's wavelength, putting Tyndall's observation on a mathematical footing.

provenance.author: J. W. Strutt (Lord Rayleigh)
provenance.title: On the light from the sky, its polarization and colour
provenance.publisher: The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science, Series 4

nodes.title: Rayleigh scattering law
nodes.summary: For particles much smaller than the wavelength of light, the intensity of scattered light depends on the particle's size and refractive index and, steeply, on the wavelength of the light.

provenance.author: J. W. Strutt (Lord Rayleigh)
provenance.title: On the scattering of light by small particles
provenance.publisher: The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science, Series 4

nodes.title: The lambda^-4 law
nodes.summary: Rayleigh-scattering intensity is proportional to 1/wavelength^4 (I_scattered is proportional to lambda^-4), holding the particle's size, distance, and refractive index fixed. This is the steep wavelength dependence Rayleigh derived in the scattering paper.

provenance.author: J. W. Strutt (Lord Rayleigh)
provenance.title: On the scattering of light by small particles
provenance.publisher: The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science, Series 4

nodes.title: Blue scatters far more than red
nodes.summary: Comparing violet/blue light (about 400 nm) to red light (about 700 nm) through the lambda^-4 law: (700/400)^4 is about 9.4, so short wavelengths scatter close to an order of magnitude more than long ones.

nodes.title: Why the sky reads as blue and not violet
nodes.summary: Sunlight scatters violet even more than blue, but the sky reads as blue because the Sun emits less violet than blue, the upper atmosphere absorbs some violet, and human eyes are more sensitive to blue than violet.

nodes.title: Why the sky is blue
nodes.summary: Rayleigh scattering by air molecules, molecules much smaller than light's wavelength, scatters short (blue/violet) wavelengths far more than long (red) ones. Scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every direction in the sky, which is why the sky looks blue.
